draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s actions at school cause B to transfer because A bullied or harassed B?"}
review: This is a plausible but overly specific first question: the prompt only says A caused B to transfer, not that bullying or harassment was involved. Ask a broader discriminating question instead: “Was B’s transfer caused by A’s deliberate action?” This tests intent without presuming the mechanism. There is no prior visible history to avoid repeating or revisiting.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s transfer caused by a deliberate action by A?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A deliberately bully or harass B, causing B to transfer schools?"}
review: The prior answer establishes only that A deliberately did something that caused B to transfer; it does not establish bullying or harassment. The proposal repeats that premise while adding an unsupported motive/mechanism. Better question: “Did A’s deliberate action directly target B, rather than causing B’s transfer as an indirect consequence?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s deliberate action directly target B, rather than causing B to transfer as an indirect consequence?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B to transfer because B was inadvertently affected by an incident at school?"}
review: The proposal is too specific: the history supports that A acted deliberately and that B was not the direct target, but it does not establish an incident or that B was inadvertently affected. Ask instead: “Did A’s deliberate action lead the school to make a decision that caused B to transfer?” This tests one possible indirect route without assuming an accident or particular mechanism. No repeated or rejected hypothesis appears in the visible history.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s deliberate action lead the school to make a decision that caused B to transfer?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B’s family or guardians to decide to move B to another school?"}
review: The proposal is plausible, but it assumes a specific mechanism: that B’s family or guardians made the transfer decision. The history only establishes that A’s deliberate action indirectly caused the transfer and that the school itself did not decide it. A less leading discriminator would be: “Was the transfer decision made by B or someone close to B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the decision for B to transfer made by B or someone close to B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s deliberate action aimed at someone other than B?"}
review: The proposed question overcommits: “aimed at someone other than B” assumes A’s action had a specific person as its target. The history only establishes that the action deliberately caused the transfer, did not directly target B, and did not cause a school decision; it does not identify the action’s target or mechanism. Ask instead: “Did A’s action cause the transfer through an effect on someone other than B?” That tests the third-party-consequence possibility without assuming intent. The “irrelevant” feedback does not establish who made the transfer decision.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause the transfer through an effect on someone other than B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause another student to transfer, and did B transfer in order to accompany that student?"}
review: The proposal is plausible, but it bundles two unconfirmed claims: that the other person also transferred, and that B transferred specifically to accompany them. The history only establishes that A’s action affected someone besides B and thereby caused B’s transfer; it does not identify that person or how the effect led to B leaving. Ask: “Did A’s action also cause another person to transfer schools?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action also cause another person to transfer schools?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action affect a teacher or school employee, and did that person’s response cause B to transfer?"}
review: The proposal narrows “someone other than B” to a teacher or school employee without support. The earlier “no” rules out the school’s decision causing the transfer, but does not establish—or rule out—an employee’s personal response. The question also bundles who was affected with how that person caused the transfer. Better ask: “Was the person affected by A personally connected to B, rather than involved in an official school capacity?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person affected by A’s action personally connected to B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person affected by A’s action a member of B’s family?"}
review: No hypothesis has been repeated or rejected in the visible history. Asking whether the person was family is a reasonable way to test one kind of personal connection, but the history does not specifically support family; “personally connected” could mean many things. A clearer question would be: “Was that person related to B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person affected by A’s action related to B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person affected by A’s action B’s sibling?"}
review: The history establishes only that the person affected was related to B; it gives no reason to single out a sibling. The sibling question is new, not a repeated or already rejected hypothesis, but it’s an arbitrary narrowing. A broader discriminator would be: “Was the person affected by A’s action an immediate family member of B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the person affected by A’s action an immediate family member of B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member affected by A’s action one of B’s parents?"}
review: The parent hypothesis is unsupported: “immediate family” could mean a sibling or another close relative, and nothing so far identifies which. Ask a broader causal-path question instead: “Did that family member’s response to A’s action lead to B’s transfer, rather than a direct practical consequence of the action?” The history establishes an effect on a relative, but not how that effect prompted B to leave.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the family member’s reaction to A’s action prompt B to transfer?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s deliberate action physically harm B’s immediate family member?"}
review: The proposed question adds an unsupported mechanism: nothing so far says A physically harmed the relative. The history only establishes that A’s deliberate action affected B’s immediate family member, and that this effect—not the relative’s reaction to A—caused B’s transfer. It also rules out A directly targeting B and A prompting a school decision. A less assumptive discriminator: “Did the family member’s own subsequent relocation lead B to transfer?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the family member’s own subsequent relocation lead B to transfer?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member affected by A’s action one of B’s parents?"}
review: The parent hypothesis is possible, but nothing in the history singles out a parent; “immediate family” could also mean a sibling, spouse, or child. The feedback rules out the family member’s reaction and their own relocation as the cause of B’s transfer, so don’t revive either route. A broader, more discriminating question: **Did A’s action cause the family member to face a serious consequence that changed B’s circumstances?**
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B’s family member to face a serious consequence that changed B’s circumstances?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B’s immediate family member to be arrested or imprisoned?"}
review: The history supports that A’s action affected B’s immediate family member and caused a serious consequence that changed B’s circumstances. It does not establish that the consequence was arrest or imprisonment; that is an unsupported, overly specific mechanism. The prior questions also rule out the family member’s reaction or relocation as the cause of B’s transfer. A better discriminator is: “Was the serious consequence a legal consequence for B’s family member?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the serious consequence a legal consequence for B’s family member?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B’s family member to be arrested or prosecuted for a crime?"}
review: The proposed question assumes a specific criminal process—arrest or prosecution—that the history does not establish. We know only that A’s action caused a serious legal consequence for B’s immediate family member. A better discriminating question is: “Was that legal consequence criminal in nature, rather than civil or administrative?” The history already rules out direct targeting of B, a school decision caused by A, the relative’s reaction or relocation, and another person transferring; avoid revisiting those explanations.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the legal consequence for B’s family member criminal in nature, rather than civil or administrative?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s family member sentenced to prison as a result of A’s action?"}
review: The history supports a serious criminal legal consequence for B’s immediate family member, but not a prison sentence specifically. The proposed question is plausible and not repeated, yet it assumes a particular outcome. A cleaner discriminator is: “Did the consequence include the family member actually being imprisoned, rather than only being investigated, arrested, or charged?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the criminal consequence include B’s family member actually being imprisoned, rather than only being investigated, arrested, or charged?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause B’s family member to be criminally prosecuted for a crime that the family member had committed?"}
review: The history establishes a criminal legal consequence, but not prosecution or that the family member actually committed an offense. The proposed question bundles those assumptions. Ask instead: “Was B’s family member actually guilty of the offense underlying the criminal consequence?” This tests culpability without presuming a particular procedural stage or mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did B’s family member actually commit the crime that led to the criminal consequence?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member B’s parent?"}
review: “Parent?” is a possible test, but nothing in the history favors a parent over another immediate family member. More importantly, it narrows the relationship without clarifying how A’s action led to the legal consequence. Ask instead: “Did A’s action cause the family member to commit the crime, rather than expose or report a crime they had already committed?” That tests a still-unresolved causal link; the history establishes the consequence and that the family member committed the crime, but not how A’s action related to it.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action cause the family member to commit the crime, rather than expose or report a crime they had already committed?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member B’s parent?"}
review: The parent hypothesis is unsupported: the history establishes only that the affected person was B’s immediate family member, not which relation. The last answer also does not prove A reported the crime; “no” to causing it leaves other possibilities. A better discriminating question is: “Did A’s action bring the family member’s already-committed crime to the attention of authorities?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s action bring the family member’s already-committed crime to the attention of the authorities?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}
review: The parent question is a valid, unasked possibility, but nothing in the history identifies which immediate family member it was. A more informative next question would clarify A’s role in the crime coming to light: “Did A intentionally report or provide information about the family member’s crime to authorities, rather than the authorities discovering it another way?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A deliberately give authorities information that exposed the family member’s already-committed crime?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}
review: The parent hypothesis is not repeated or rejected: the history establishes only that the affected person was an immediate family member, not which one. Asking whether they were a parent is plausible, but it narrows the relationship without support and may not explain why B transferred. A more discriminating question would be: “Did the exposure of the crime lead to social consequences for B that prompted the transfer, rather than a change in the family’s practical circumstances?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A’s disclosure cause B to face stigma or bullying that prompted B to transfer schools?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}
review: The parent question is permissible but unsupported: the history establishes only that the person was a related immediate family member, not which one. It also does not establish imprisonment; that was explicitly marked irrelevant. Avoid building a final explanation around either assumption. The history already rules out the family member’s reaction, their relocation, and stigma or bullying as the transfer mechanism. A more useful next question is: “Did the criminal consequence leave the family member unable to care for B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the criminal consequence leave the family member unable to care for B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}
review: The history establishes only that the person was B’s immediate family member; it does not establish that they were a parent. The proposed question is a fair direct test, not a fact to build into the story, and it has not already been asked or rejected. If you want a less speculative next step, ask: “Did the family member’s criminal consequence change B’s living situation in a way that prompted the transfer?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the family member’s criminal consequence change B’s living situation in a way that prompted the transfer?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}
review: The history establishes that the relative was an immediate family member, but not that they were a parent. The proposed question is a valid test of that possibility, not a conclusion; it does not repeat an earlier question or contradict a rejected hypothesis. Ask it as written, and don’t infer a parental relationship unless confirmed.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the family member whose crime A exposed one of B’s parents?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was the parent whose crime A exposed B’s father?"}
review: The proposed question is a fair discriminator: the history establishes that the family member was one of B’s parents, but does not establish which parent. It does not repeat an already rejected hypothesis. To avoid unnecessary presupposition, ask: “Was the parent whose crime A exposed B’s father?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the parent whose crime A exposed B’s father?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A actually kill B?"}
review: “Did A actually kill B?” is a fair, unanswered question: the opening says only that A was arrested on suspicion, and no earlier question establishes B’s fate or A’s guilt. Don’t treat the arrest as proof. It is relevant to the ending, though it won’t clarify the already-established school-transfer chain: A exposed a parent’s crime, the criminal consequence changed B’s living situation, and that led to the transfer. The history rules out direct targeting of B, school action, stigma/bullying, and the family member’s reaction or relocation as the transfer mechanism. I’d ask the proposed question if resolving the disappearance is the priority.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A actually kill B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B’s parent go to prison after A reported the crime?"}
review: The proposed question repeats a point the history already marks irrelevant: whether B’s parent was actually imprisoned. Don’t infer imprisonment from the confirmed criminal consequence. A better discriminator is: “Did the parent’s legal consequences cause B to live in a different household, prompting the transfer?” The history confirms a change in B’s living situation but not that particular mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the parent’s legal consequences cause B to move into a different household, prompting the transfer?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B move into foster care or another form of state-arranged care after the parent’s legal consequences?"}
review: The proposed foster-care question is plausible, but nothing in the history establishes state involvement; “a different household” could mean a relative or the other parent. Ask instead: “Who did B move in with after the parent’s legal consequences?” This identifies the missing link without presuming a specific placement. The history already establishes that A exposed a parent’s pre-existing crime, the legal consequences changed B’s living situation and prompted the transfer, and A did not kill B. Other suggested routes—stigma or bullying, the family member’s reaction or relocation, and inability to care for B—were rejected or marked irrelevant.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did B move in with a relative after the parent’s legal consequences?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"When they reunited at university, did B know that A had exposed B’s parent’s crime?"}
review: The proposed question is not already covered, but it assumes B’s knowledge at the university reunion matters; the history doesn’t establish that, and an answer may not explain B’s later disappearance. The history does establish that A exposed a parent’s crime, B then moved in with a relative and transferred, and A did not kill B. A more discriminating next question is: “Did B disappear voluntarily?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did B disappear voluntarily?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B disappear deliberately to make it look as though A had murdered B?"}
review: The history establishes that B disappeared voluntarily and that A did not kill B, but it does not establish that B intended to frame A. The proposed question adds that specific motive. A more discriminating, less assumptive question is: “Did B’s disappearance itself lead the authorities to suspect A?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did B’s disappearance itself lead the authorities to suspect A?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B disappear to escape A or their marriage?"}
review: The proposed question assumes B fled A or the marriage, but nothing in the history establishes that; the loving-couple detail doesn’t rule it out either. The history already establishes that B disappeared voluntarily and that the disappearance itself did not lead authorities to suspect A. A less leading discriminator is: “Was B’s voluntary disappearance motivated by something A did after they reunited?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s voluntary disappearance motivated by something A did after they reunited?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B deliberately make the disappearance look like A had murdered B, causing A to be arrested?"}
review: Reject this proposal: it conflicts with the explicit “no” that B’s disappearance itself led authorities to suspect A. The history also says B’s voluntary disappearance was not motivated by anything A did after they reunited, but it does not establish that B staged evidence or intended to frame A. Ask instead: “Did authorities suspect A because of evidence or information independent of B’s disappearance?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did authorities suspect A because of evidence or information independent of B’s disappearance?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B voluntarily disappear in order to escape or avoid someone other than A?"}
review: The proposed question assumes an escape motive and an identifiable person B was avoiding. The history establishes only that B disappeared voluntarily and that A’s actions after their reunion did not motivate it; neither fact implies B was fleeing anyone. A more neutral discriminator is: “Did B plan the disappearance in advance?” This tests an aspect of the voluntary disappearance without presuming why B left. Also, the record says authorities suspected A based on information independent of the disappearance, so don’t treat the disappearance itself as the reason for the arrest.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did B plan the disappearance in advance?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A suspected because physical evidence of a violent crime involving B was found?"}
review: The proposed question assumes a violent crime involving B occurred and that physical evidence was found; the history establishes neither. It also risks treating suspicion as proof B was harmed, despite the answer that B disappeared voluntarily and A did not kill B. A better discriminator is: “Was the independent evidence that led authorities to suspect A connected to A’s own conduct, rather than to evidence that B had been harmed?” This hasn’t been asked already and avoids guessing at a specific mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was the independent information that led authorities to suspect A based on something A had done or said?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A give the authorities a false account of what happened to B?"}
review: The proposed question is too specific: nothing established so far says A gave authorities an account about B, much less a false one. The history does establish that suspicion came from information independent of B’s disappearance and based on something A did or said. No earlier question has tested whether that information was something A told authorities. Ask: “Did authorities suspect A because of a statement A made to them about B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did authorities suspect A because of a statement A made to them about B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A tell the authorities that A had killed B?"}
review: This is a reasonable discriminating question: the history establishes that A made a statement to authorities about B, but not what A said. A’s actual killing of B has already been rejected, so a “yes” would indicate a false claim or some other nonliteral statement—not that A really killed B. You could make that distinction explicit: “Did A falsely tell the authorities that A had killed B?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A falsely tell the authorities that A had killed B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A falsely claim to have killed B in order to protect B or help B remain missing?"}
review: The proposed question is not a repeat, but it bundles two specific motives—protecting B and helping B stay missing—that the history does not establish. B’s disappearance was voluntary and not motivated by something A did after they reunited; that still does not tell us why A falsely confessed. A cleaner discriminator is: “Was A’s false claim meant to mislead investigators about B’s whereabouts?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s false claim meant to mislead investigators about B’s whereabouts?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A falsely claim to have killed B in order to protect B from some other consequence?"}
review: The proposed question is not a repeat: the history only rules out that A’s false claim was meant to mislead investigators about B’s whereabouts. But “some other consequence” assumes a specific protective motive and an additional consequence that the clues haven’t established. A cleaner probe is: **“Was A’s false confession intended to protect B?”** This tests the broader motive without guessing how. Note that earlier “irrelevant” answers do not establish a particular explanation.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s false claim motivated by a desire to protect B?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A falsely claim to have killed B because A felt guilty about exposing B’s parent’s crime and causing the disruption in B’s childhood?"}
review: The proposal turns an unconfirmed motive into a specific explanation. The history establishes that A exposed B’s parent’s crime, contributing to B’s move and transfer, but says nothing about whether A felt guilty. It also rules out two nearby motives: A’s false claim was not meant to mislead investigators about B’s whereabouts and was not motivated by a desire to protect B. A useful discriminating question is: “Was A’s false confession motivated by guilt over A’s earlier role in disrupting B’s life?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s false confession motivated by guilt over A’s earlier role in disrupting B’s life?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A make the false confession to attract attention or notoriety?"}
review: The proposed question tests a motive not already covered, but “attention or notoriety” is a specific, unsupported explanation. The history rules out misleading investigators about B’s whereabouts, protecting B, and guilt over A’s earlier role; it does not establish why A confessed. A broader discriminator would be: “Was A’s false confession intended to achieve a particular goal for A?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s false confession intended to achieve a particular goal for A?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s goal in falsely confessing to secure some benefit or outcome for A personally?"}
review: The proposed question is not a repeat, but “some benefit or outcome … personally” is so broad that a yes may add little beyond the established fact that A had a goal. Ask a more discriminating, still open-ended category question: **“Was A trying to avoid a legal consequence for A?”** That tests one possible kind of personal goal without assuming a particular offense, motive, or outcome. Nothing in the history establishes that this is the answer.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to avoid a legal consequence for A?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s false confession intended to gain public attention or notoriety?"}
review:
The proposed question is possible, but public attention or notoriety is unsupported so far. The history establishes only that A’s false confession served a particular goal; it already rules out avoiding a legal consequence, protecting B, misleading investigators about B’s whereabouts, and guilt over A’s earlier role. Don’t treat those exclusions as evidence for notoriety.

A broader next question: “Was A’s goal in confessing to cause someone else to take a particular action?” This can distinguish an intended effect on another person from a goal centered on A, without presuming what either goal was.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s goal in confessing to cause someone else to take a particular action?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s goal to make B come out of hiding or otherwise reveal where B was?"}
review: The proposed question assumes B was “in hiding,” which the public history does not establish. It also comes close to the already-rejected idea that A’s confession was meant to mislead investigators about B’s whereabouts; that “no” does not rule out every possible motive involving B, but makes this specific guess weak. A better discriminator is: **Was A trying to induce someone other than B to take a particular action?** The existing “yes” only says A wanted someone else to act, and does not identify whether that person was B or another person.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to induce someone other than B to take a particular action?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to make B reappear by falsely confessing to B’s murder?"}
review: The history supports that A’s confession aimed to make someone act, and the answer was “no” when asked whether that person was someone other than B. It does not establish that A wanted B to reappear. Earlier answers also rule out misleading investigators about B’s whereabouts and protecting B, but don’t settle what action A hoped B would take. A cleaner next question is: “Was A trying to induce B to end the disappearance?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to induce B to end the disappearance?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B voluntarily disappear to escape or avoid a problem in B’s own life?"}
review: The proposed question has not been asked or rejected, but “a problem in B’s own life” is vague and may bundle very different motives. The history establishes that B disappeared voluntarily and that A’s later actions did not motivate it; it does not establish why B disappeared. A clearer discriminator: “Was B trying to avoid an immediate danger to themself?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B trying to avoid an immediate danger to themself?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did B disappear in order to start a new life under a different identity?"}
review: The proposed question is unsupported: voluntary disappearance doesn’t establish that B adopted a different identity, and the history hasn’t established B’s motive. Nothing already asked directly covers whether B intended a permanent break from their old life. A broader, discriminating question would be: “Was B’s disappearance intended to make a permanent break from their previous life?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s disappearance intended to make a permanent break from their previous life?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Did A believe B would learn of the false confession and come forward to prevent A from being convicted?"}
review: The proposed question is plausible but overcommits: nothing establishes that B would learn of the confession, come forward specifically to prevent a conviction, or that A expected that exact chain. The “no” to A trying to avoid a legal consequence also cautions against framing conviction avoidance as A’s motive. The history already establishes that A’s goal was to induce B to end the disappearance, so don’t repeat that. A more discriminating, less assumptive question: “Did A expect B to respond to the confession by contacting A directly?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did A expect B to respond to the confession by contacting A directly?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s purpose in falsely confessing to make B feel compelled to reveal that they were alive in order to save A from being wrongly punished?"}
review: The proposed question rests on a premise the history already rejects: A was **not** trying to avoid a legal consequence for themself. Saying A wanted B to appear so A would not be wrongly punished is essentially that same motive, so it is unlikely to discriminate. Also, whether A expected B to contact A directly was marked irrelevant; don’t assume that was the intended response. A safer next question is: “Was A trying to get B to reappear or resume contact with someone other than A?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to get B to reappear publicly or contact someone other than A?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s goal in making the false confession to resume a romantic relationship with B?"}
review: The romantic motive has not been established, but this question is not a repeat of an earlier one: the history only confirms A wanted B to end the disappearance. Ask: “Was A’s aim specifically to rekindle their marriage, rather than simply to make B reappear?” Treat either answer as a new clue, not confirmation of a broader motive.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to get B to resume their marriage?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A trying to provoke B into reappearing by making B believe A would suffer a serious consequence?"}
review: The proposal adds an unsupported mechanism: nothing establishes that A wanted B to believe A would suffer a serious consequence. The history only confirms that A falsely confessed, hoping to make B end the disappearance; A was not trying to avoid a legal consequence. The earlier questions about whether B would contact A, reappear publicly, or contact someone else were answered “irrelevant,” which does not establish any of those details. A more discriminating question would be: “Was A hoping B would reappear and tell the authorities that A’s confession was false?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was A hoping B would reappear and tell the authorities that A’s confession was false?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s disappearance connected to the parent whose crime A had exposed?"}
review: This is a useful, non-repeated question: the history establishes that the parent’s crime and legal consequences changed B’s living situation, but does not establish any link to B’s later disappearance. “Connected” is vague, though. A clearer discriminator: “Did the parent’s crime or its legal consequences contribute to B’s decision to disappear?” This tests the connection without assuming a particular motive or mechanism.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Did the parent’s crime or its legal consequences contribute to B’s decision to disappear?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s parent imprisoned for a crime involving the death of another person?"}
review: The proposed question adds an unestablished detail: no feedback indicates the parent’s crime involved someone’s death. Imprisonment has already been tested and marked irrelevant, so making it part of the question is especially unlikely to discriminate. A broader next question could be: “Did B disappear because they feared consequences for themself connected to the parent’s crime?” The history establishes only that the parent committed a crime A exposed, its legal consequences changed B’s living situation, and it contributed to B’s disappearance—not the crime’s type or whether the parent was imprisoned.
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s disappearance partly motivated by fear of being implicated in the parent’s crime?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s disappearance motivated by shame or emotional distress connected to the parent’s crime or its consequences?"}
review: The proposal is plausible but “shame” is an unsupported, specific motive; the history only establishes that the parent’s crime or its consequences contributed to the disappearance and rules out fear of being implicated. Emotional distress is also unconfirmed. This has not already been asked. A cleaner discriminating question: “Was B’s disappearance motivated by emotional distress over the parent’s crime or its consequences?”
action: {"type":"question","text":"Was B’s disappearance motivated by emotional distress over the parent’s crime or its consequences?"}

draft: {"type":"question","text":"Was A’s goal in getting B to reappear related to a legal matter involving B?"}
review: The proposed question assumes a legal matter involving B, which the history doesn’t establish; the known legal thread is the parent’s crime and A’s false confession. Also, A’s motive has already been explored: A hoped B would reappear and tell authorities the confession was false, and A was not trying to avoid a legal consequence.
